interactions.title: Permission calculator and access check
interactions.description: Type a mode or tick the bits, pick who is asking and what they want to do, then step through the kernel's decision: one class, one bit, allowed or denied.

interactions.title: Follow the data through a pipeline
interactions.description: Each stage of a real pipeline on the practice-lab files, with the exact output that flows into the next command.

interactions.title: Where do stdout and stderr go?
interactions.description: ls prints one line to stdout and one error to stderr. Choose a redirection and watch the shell rewire file descriptors from left to right.

interactions.title: A process changes state
interactions.description: Follow one process through fork and exec, sleeping, stopping, uninterruptible I/O, becoming a zombie and being reaped — with the ps line at every step.

interactions.title: Send signals to a process
interactions.description: Send SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGHUP, SIGSTOP, SIGCONT and SIGKILL to a plain process, one that traps signals, one that ignores them, and a zombie.

interactions.title: Build a find command
interactions.description: Combine name, type, size and age tests and watch find test every entry of the practice lab — including why -size -1k matches only empty files.

interactions.title: sed substitution, line by line
interactions.description: Write an s/pattern/replacement/ command with an address and flags, and see which lines are selected, where the pattern matches and what sed prints.

interactions.title: Hard links vs symbolic links
interactions.description: Create a file, a hard link and a symlink, then edit, delete and recreate the original. Watch directory entries, inodes and link counts.

interactions.title: Investigate a full disk
interactions.description: A simulated server is out of disk space. Choose each next command; wrong choices explain why they do not help.

interactions.title: A service fails: port already in use
interactions.description: A service will not start after a deployment. Read the status, find who holds the port, identify it and fix it safely.

interactions.title: Predict the output: quoting and expansion
interactions.description: Run in ~/linux-lab, where config/ contains app.conf and db.conf.

questions.prompt: What does the second command print?
questions.explanation: Single quotes keep every character literally, so no variable expansion happens.

options: Linux lab has $(ls config | wc -l) files
questions.explanation: Double quotes allow variable expansion and command substitution, but prevent word splitting and globbing.

questions.prompt: A file named "a b.txt" exists. What happens?
options: ls reports two errors: 'a' and 'b.txt' do not exist
questions.explanation: The unquoted $f is split on the space into two arguments, a and b.txt. Write ls "$f".
Globs are not expanded inside quotes. Unquoted, the shell replaces the pattern with the matching file names before echo runs.
Brace expansion generates one word per value, each with the suffix attached.

options: Every 15 minutes between 09:00 and 17:45, Monday to Friday
Every 15 minutes from 9 to 17 on the 1st–5th of each month
questions.explanation: Minute */15 (0, 15, 30, 45) of every hour from 9 to 17 inclusive, on days of week 1–5. The last run is 17:45.
The order is minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week; Sunday is 0 (or 7).

options: 09:00 on the first Monday of each month
09:00 on the 1st of each month and every Monday
questions.explanation: When both day of month and day of week are restricted, cron runs when EITHER matches.

questions.prompt: This job never creates its file: `0 1 * * * tar -czf /backup/home-$(date +%F).tar.gz /home`. Why?
options: An unescaped % ends the command in a crontab line; write \%
questions.explanation: In crontab lines % becomes a newline and the rest is sent as standard input. Escape it as \% or move the command into a script.
